# ScreenTinker

> Open-source digital signage. A self-hostable CMS and player fleet manager, MIT licensed, with an optional hosted version. Runs on Android TV and Fire TV, Amazon Vega OS, Samsung Tizen, LG webOS, BrightSign, Raspberry Pi, Windows, ChromeOS, any web browser, and e-paper/ESP32 panels driven by a server-side renderer — eleven platforms, one CMS.

ScreenTinker turns ordinary screens into managed digital signs. A server holds the content, playlists, layouts and schedules; players pair to it and pull what they should be showing. The player is a web page, so a display that can open a URL can run it, and native builds exist for the platforms that need one.

The whole project is MIT licensed and self-hosting is free. A paid hosted version runs the same software on our infrastructure for people who would rather not maintain a server. There is no hosted-only feature set.

## Start here

- [ScreenTinker home](https://screentinker.com/): what it is, features, pricing, and platform support.
- [What is digital signage?](https://screentinker.com/guides/what-is-digital-signage.html): plain-language explanation of how signage works, what it displays, and what it costs.
- [Open source digital signage software](https://screentinker.com/guides/open-source-digital-signage.html): the licence, the data-ownership argument, and where ScreenTinker fits.
- [Certified Hardware](https://screentinker.com/certified-hardware): the device models ByteTinker has tested, what each one does, which are only community-reported, and which are not supported and why.

## Choosing how to run it

- [Self-hosted digital signage: complete guide](https://screentinker.com/guides/self-hosted-digital-signage.html): hardware, deployment, reverse proxy and TLS, running it as a service, and backups.
- [Hosted digital signage platform](https://screentinker.com/cloud-digital-signage.html): the cloud version, what it does and does not change, and an honest account of when self-hosting is the better answer.

## Player setup by platform

Every platform has a guide, and every player is downloaded from the instance that will run it — see
[Downloads](https://screentinker.com/download/), which lists what a given server actually has and says
so plainly when it has none.

- [Digital signage on a Raspberry Pi](https://screentinker.com/guides/raspberry-pi-digital-signage.html)
- [Digital signage for Android TV and Fire TV](https://screentinker.com/guides/digital-signage-android-tv.html)
- [Samsung TV digital signage without MagicINFO](https://screentinker.com/guides/samsung-tv-digital-signage.html): uses the built-in URL Launcher, and states which model years actually work.
- [LG webOS Signage panels](https://screentinker.com/guides/lg-webos-digital-signage.html): the .ipk, USB or SI-server install, fleet provisioning and self-update. Community-reported, not certified.
- [BrightSign players](https://screentinker.com/guides/brightsign-digital-signage.html): one autorun.zip built by your own server, dual output, BrightWall sync, real reboots and CEC panel power.
- [Digital signage on Windows](https://screentinker.com/guides/windows-digital-signage.html): kiosk-mode browser, autostart, and the settings that decide whether it survives a month.
- [ChromeOS and Chromebox](https://screentinker.com/guides/chromeos-digital-signage.html): managed kiosk through the Google Admin console, or unmanaged on a single device.
- [Fire TV Stick 4K Select and HD (Vega OS)](https://screentinker.com/guides/digital-signage-vega.html): these two sticks are not Android, the APK does not install, and they are **not** certified hardware.
- [E-paper and ESP32 signs](https://screentinker.com/guides/eink-esp32-digital-signage.html): no browser on the
  device. The server renders, dithers and packs each frame and tells the board how long to deep sleep; a 304
  when nothing changed means the panel is never refreshed for nothing. Ten panel presets, Floyd–Steinberg
  and Atkinson dithering.
- [LED walls](https://screentinker.com/guides/led-wall-digital-signage.html): there is no LED-wall integration
  and none is needed — the controller presents the wall as one display. ⚠️ Bezel compensation should be
  OFF: LED tiles are seamless and compensating for a gap that is not there crops the content.

## Project and API

- [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/screentinker/screentinker): MIT licensed, issues and releases.
- [REST API reference](https://screentinker.com/docs): the OpenAPI specification, rendered.
- [OpenAPI description](https://screentinker.com/openapi.yaml): the machine-readable contract.
- [API catalogue](https://screentinker.com/.well-known/api-catalog): RFC 9727 linkset.
- [How to authenticate](https://screentinker.com/.well-known/auth.md): scoped bearer tokens, what they can and cannot reach, and how a human creates one.

## Acting on a ScreenTinker instance as an agent

- **This software runs an MCP server.** Every instance, hosted or self-hosted, serves the Model Context
  Protocol at `/mcp`. Point an MCP client at it with `Authorization: Bearer st_...` and you get a curated
  set of twenty-one tools rather than 133 raw endpoints.
- [Manage your screens from Claude](https://screentinker.com/guides/mcp-digital-signage.html): setup, the
  tool list by scope, and how it is kept safe.
- ⚠️ The tool list is filtered by the token's scope: a `read` token is never shown a tool that writes.
- ⚠️ Playlist edits are a DRAFT until published. An agent that adds items and stops has changed nothing
  that appears on a screen.

## Reading this site as an agent

- Every published page has a **Markdown rendition**: append `.md` to its path, or send
  `Accept: text/markdown`. Responses carry `Link` headers pointing at the catalogue, the OpenAPI
  description and this file.
- `robots.txt` carries Content Signals: `search=yes, ai-input=yes, ai-train=yes`. Quoting and
  summarising this site is welcome; attribution to https://screentinker.com is appreciated.
- ⚠️ There is no way for an agent to obtain an API token on its own. A human creates one in the
  dashboard. An instance that appears to offer one is not ours.
